content: 1. Tuberculin is a diagnostic agent approved by the FDA for the detection of tuberculosis (TB) infection. 2. Common adverse reactions to tuberculin include redness at the injection site, fainting (syncope), and hypersensitivity reactions. 3. TUBERSOL, a purified protein derivative (PPD) of tuberculin, is indicated for diagnosing TB infection in individuals at increased risk of developing active TB disease. 4. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have published guidelines identifying populations that would benefit from tuberculin skin testing (TST). 5. A history of Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination is not a contraindication for tuberculin testing. Skin test results in BCG-vaccinated individuals can help support or exclude a TB diagnosis. 6. For individuals aged 5 years and older who have received BCG vaccination, an FDA-approved interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) is preferred over the tuberculin skin test. 7. The standard dose for intradermal (Mantoux) testing is 1 mL of tuberculin. 8. There is limited information regarding off-label use of tuberculin in both adult and pediatric patients, whether guideline-supported or not. 9. Contraindications to TUBERSOL include allergy to any component of the product, a history of anaphylactic or other severe allergic reactions to previous tuberculin tests, active TB, prior treatment for TB, and conditions such as extensive burns or eczema. 10. Epinephrine and other agents for managing immediate allergic reactions must be readily available during administration. 11. Syncope (fainting) can occur with injectable medications, including TUBERSOL. Measures should be in place to prevent injury and restore blood flow to the brain in such cases. 12. The expected reaction for a positive skin test is induration (hardening) at the injection site. 13. Adverse events reported include injection site pain, itching, discomfort, redness, rash, hemorrhage, hematoma, vesicles, ulcers, necrosis, scarring, fever, hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., anaphylaxis, angioedema, urticaria), respiratory symptoms (e.g., stridor, dyspnea), generalized rash, and syncope with or without seizure-like activity. 14. Reactivity to the tuberculin test may be suppressed in individuals receiving corticosteroids, immunosuppressive agents, or certain live virus vaccines. Testing should be delayed for at least one month after live virus vaccination. 15. Simultaneous administration of TUBERSOL and live attenuated virus vaccines is possible if given at separate sites. 16. Tuberculin is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA, meaning its effects on fetal harm or reproductive capacity are unknown. It should only be used in pregnant women if clearly needed. 17. There is no FDA guidance on the use of tuberculin during labor and delivery, in nursing mothers, or in specific populations such as geriatric patients, individuals with renal or hepatic impairment, or immunocompromised patients. 18. Tuberculin is administered via intradermal injection only. Intravenous, intramuscular, or subcutaneous administration is not appropriate. 19. The preferred site for the Mantoux test is the volar aspect of the forearm, avoiding areas of redness, swelling, or visible veins. 20. Proper technique involves cleaning the skin, using a calibrated syringe with a short needle, and injecting the dose intradermally to form a pale bleb approximately 10 mm in diameter. 21. If no bleb forms during injection, the test should be repeated at a different site. 22. Patients must return within 48 to 72 hours for the test to be read by a trained healthcare professional. Self-reading is discouraged. 23. The test is interpreted based on the presence and size of induration, measured transversely to the forearm's long axis in millimeters. Redness is not measured. 24. Positive reactions may indicate latent TB infection, prior TB infection, or disease but do not necessarily confirm active TB. 25. False-negative reactions can occur, particularly in elderly individuals, those tested for the first time, or those with altered immune status. 26. Tuberculin sensitivity may take up to 8 weeks to develop after exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Retesting is recommended 8-10 weeks after the last known exposure. 27. Impaired cell-mediated immunity (CMI) can lead to false-negative results. Testing should be deferred in patients with major viral infections or recent live-virus vaccination. 28. Tuberculin sensitivity in HIV-infected individuals is less reliable as CD4 counts decline, so testing should be performed early after HIV infection. 29. Tuberculin works by stimulating sensitized T lymphocytes, which mediate a delayed hypersensitivity reaction. This reaction peaks at 48-72 hours and subsides over days. 30. The immune response consists of induration due to cell infiltration and, in some cases, vesiculation or necrosis. 31. Tuberculin is a clear, colorless liquid, and each lot is tested for potency against the US Standard Tuberculin PPD-S. 32. Tuberculin should be stored at 2°C to 8°C (35°F to 46°F), protected from light, and discarded if exposed to freezing or after 30 days of use. 33. There is no established interaction between alcohol and tuberculin. Patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol use with this medication.
